Energy flows of the dryer process (Corrugated-conventional process) However, other steam and electricity consumptions in the conventional drying process still need to be considered, such as the steam required for air heating and ventilation systems, which can support the heat recovery captured from exhaust air to raise the temperature of supply air to the hood temperature and remove the air moisture. The investigation of defining how and where US and RF can be integrated efficiently within the drying process was conducted. Consequently, it is significant to understand the importance of controlling the heating rate by optimizing the drying sequence, which is essential for machine runnability. This is critical to prevent excessive adhesion of the wet web to cylinders in the early stages of drying that would cause web breaks and to maximize the drying rate at later stages when the remaining water is more tightly bound to the fibers. Therefore, the drying process is characterized by three periods (initial heat-up period, constant rate period, and falling rate period) representing the heating sequence used to efficiently remove water in its various forms while optimizing machine runnability, as shown in Figure 29. 40 DE-EE0009395 Figure 29. An illustrated diagram of three periods (initial heat-up period, constant rate period, falling rate period) that represent the heating sequence of a long drying section The actual paper machine case data and the experimental data (from Task 1) for using an ultrasonic transducer were selected to show the leverage of integrating ultrasonic into the conventional paper drying process. The data of the actual case study was extracted from an industrial report and used to visualize the paper drying process by dividing the process into multiple sections based on the dryer pressure and saturated steam temperature. In addition, the drying process can be divided into three periods representing the heating sequence based on the paper sheet temperature distribution along the machine, as shown in Figure 30. 41 DE-EE0009395 Figure 30. An illustrated diagram of three periods that represent the heating sequence based on the paper sheet temperature distribution along the actual paper machine case The SRNL experimental data was obtained from the data of Task 1, which used an ultrasonic transducer with 120 kHz and 36 Watts at room temperature vs. conduction drying at 95 oC at 1 sec. The obtained results from using ultrasonic drying in place of steam cylinders in the heat-up period with both 100% and 90% efficiency for ultrasonic transducers show a fairly significant reduction in the energy intensity at a reduction of about 10.8-11.3% compared to conventional drying using steam cylinders. Replacing steam cylinders with ultrasonic drying in the falling rate period with both 100% and 90% efficiency for ultrasonic transducers shows a significant reduction in the energy intensity at about 27.7-27.8% compared to the conventional drying using steam cylinders, as shown in Figure 31.
